item.title: Components of a State Park Pass Holder Survey
item.stimulus: The state park agency sold annual park passes to 48,000 people last year. The state has about 2.1 million adult residents. The agency wants to know whether its pass holders would use a proposed online campsite reservation system. Calling every pass holder would take agency staff several months, so the agency selected a random sample of 600 pass holders and asked each one: "Would you use an online campsite reservation system? (yes or no)" All 600 pass holders in the sample answered, and 372 of them answered yes.

parts.prompt: Identify the population and the sample in this study, and give the values of N and n.

criteria.text: Identifies the population as all 48,000 people who hold an annual pass from the state park agency, with N = 48,000.
criteria.evidence: Response names all of the agency's annual pass holders as the population and gives N = 48,000 (not 2.1 million and not 600).
criteria.fix: Name the whole group the agency wants to learn about, then give N as the size of that group, not a larger group.

criteria.text: Identifies the sample as the 600 randomly selected pass holders who were asked the question, with n = 600.
criteria.evidence: Response names the 600 pass holders who were selected and asked the question as the sample and gives n = 600.
criteria.fix: Name the subset of the population from which data were actually obtained, then give n as the number of individuals in it.

parts.prompt: Explain why the agency used a statistical study instead of collecting data from every pass holder.

criteria.text: Explains that collecting data from every one of the 48,000 pass holders would be too difficult or time-consuming, so data were collected from a sample instead.
criteria.evidence: Response states that contacting every pass holder is impractical because of the size of the population or the months of staff time it would take.
criteria.fix: Give a reason tied to the context: say what makes collecting data from every member of this population too large or too difficult a task.

parts.prompt: One pass holder in the sample answered yes. Identify the datum that this pass holder provides, and describe the data set that the agency collected.

criteria.text: Identifies the datum as this pass holder's answer, yes, to the question about using an online campsite reservation system.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the datum is the single recorded answer (yes) for this one pass holder, not the pass holder or the count 372.
criteria.fix: A datum is one piece of information about one individual; state the recorded answer for that individual, not the individual.

criteria.text: Describes the data set as the collection of all 600 yes-or-no answers given by the sampled pass holders.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the data set is the full collection of recorded answers from the 600 sampled pass holders.
criteria.fix: Describe the data set as the full collection of recorded values, one per sampled individual, and say how many values it contains.

item.model_answer:
(a) The population is all 48,000 people who hold an annual pass from the state park agency, so N = 48,000. The sample is the 600 randomly selected pass holders who were asked the question, so n = 600.

(b) The population of 48,000 pass holders is too large to contact everyone easily: calling every pass holder would take agency staff several months. A statistical study lets the agency collect data from a sample of 600 pass holders to answer its question about all pass holders.

(c) The datum is this pass holder's answer, yes, to the question "Would you use an online campsite reservation system?" The data set is the collection of all 600 yes-or-no answers given by the sampled pass holders (372 yes and 228 no).

n=600
residents=2_100_000
yes=372
assert n<N<residents
assert n-yes==228

item.title: Grade Group and Preferred Study Location
item.stimulus:
A high school surveyed 500 of its students about where they prefer to study. Each student was classified by grade group and by preferred study location. The results are shown in the table.

Grade group | Home | Library | Café | Total
Grades 9–10 | 156 | 52 | 52 | 260
Grades 11–12 | 96 | 84 | 60 | 240
Total | 252 | 136 | 112 | 500

parts.prompt: For these 500 students, calculate the joint relative frequency of being in grades 11–12 and preferring the library, and calculate the marginal relative frequency of preferring the library.

criteria.text: Joint relative frequency: 84/500 = 0.168.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the single cell count 84 by the table total 500 to get 0.168.
criteria.fix: For a joint relative frequency, divide the one cell count by the total for the entire table, not by a row or column total.

criteria.text: Marginal relative frequency: 136/500 = 0.272.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the Library column total 136 by the table total 500 to get 0.272.
criteria.fix: For a marginal relative frequency, divide the row or column total for that category by the total for the entire table.

parts.prompt: In grades 9–10, 52 of the 260 students (0.20) prefer the library. Calculate the proportion of students in grades 11–12 who prefer the library. Based on the conditional relative frequencies of preferred study location for the two grade groups, is there an association between grade group and preferred study location for these students? Justify your answer.

criteria.text: Calculates the conditional relative frequency 84/240 = 0.35 for students in grades 11–12 who prefer the library.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the grades 11–12 Library count 84 by the grades 11–12 row total 240 to get 0.35.
criteria.fix: To condition on grade group, divide each cell count by that grade group's row total, not by the column total or table total.

criteria.text: States that there is an association, because the conditional distributions of preferred study location differ between the grade groups, citing at least one comparison of conditional relative frequencies (for example 0.20 versus 0.35 for the library, or 0.60 versus 0.40 for home).
criteria.evidence: Response says yes, there is an association, and supports it by comparing conditional relative frequencies (not raw counts) for the two grade groups.
criteria.fix: Compare the same conditional relative frequency across the groups; if the values differ noticeably, state that the variables are associated and cite them.

parts.prompt: A student claims: "Most of the students who prefer the library are in grades 11–12." Use an appropriate relative frequency to determine whether the data support this claim.

criteria.text: Computes 84/136 ≈ 0.618, the proportion of library-preferring students who are in grades 11–12.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the grades 11–12 Library count 84 by the Library column total 136 to get about 0.618.
criteria.fix: Identify the group the claim restricts to, students who prefer the library, and divide by that group's column total.

criteria.text: Concludes that the data support the claim because 0.618 is greater than 0.5 (more than half of library-preferring students are in grades 11–12).
criteria.evidence: Response compares the conditional relative frequency it computed with 0.5 (one half) and states that the claim is supported.
criteria.fix: Most means more than half: compare the relative frequency with 0.5, then state whether the claim is supported.

item.model_answer:
(a) Joint relative frequency of grades 11–12 and library = 84/500 = 0.168.
Marginal relative frequency of library = 136/500 = 0.272.

(b) Grades 9–10: 52/260 = 0.20 prefer the library (given). Grades 11–12: 84/240 = 0.35 prefer the library.
Yes, there is an association between grade group and preferred study location for these students. The conditional distributions differ: 35% of students in grades 11–12 prefer the library compared with 20% in grades 9–10, and 60% (156/260) of students in grades 9–10 prefer home compared with 40% (96/240) in grades 11–12. If the variables were not associated, these conditional relative frequencies would be about the same for both grade groups.

(c) Among the 136 students who prefer the library, 84 are in grades 11–12, so the proportion is 84/136 ≈ 0.618. Because 0.618 is greater than 0.5, most of the students who prefer the library are in grades 11–12, so the data support the claim.

item.title: Pastry Orders and Mobile App Payments
item.stimulus:
A coffee shop recorded 800 transactions during one week. Each transaction was classified by whether the customer ordered a pastry and whether the customer paid with the shop's mobile app.

Order | Paid with app | Did not pay with app | Total
Ordered a pastry | 120 | 120 | 240
No pastry | 240 | 320 | 560
Total | 360 | 440 | 800

One of these 800 transactions is selected at random. Let A be the event that the customer ordered a pastry, and let M be the event that the customer paid with the mobile app.

parts.prompt: Find P(A ∪ M), the probability that the selected customer ordered a pastry or paid with the app (or both). Show your work.

criteria.evidence: Response shows a correct calculation that counts transactions with both a pastry and an app payment only once, or uses the complement 1 − P(no pastry and no app) = 1 − 320/800, and obtains 0.60.
criteria.fix: When adding P(A) and P(M), subtract P(A ∩ M) so that transactions with both a pastry and an app payment are counted once.

parts.prompt: Are events A and M independent? Justify your answer using probabilities.

criteria.text: Computes a pair of probabilities that would be equal if the events were independent, such as P(A | M) = 120/360 ≈ 0.333 and P(A) = 240/800 = 0.30, or P(A ∩ M) = 0.15 and P(A)·P(M) = 0.30 × 0.45 = 0.135.
criteria.evidence: Response computes both values of a valid independence check from the table (a conditional versus an unconditional probability, or a joint probability versus a product).
criteria.fix: Write the independence check first, for example P(A | M) = P(A), then compute both sides from the table.

criteria.text: Concludes that A and M are not independent because the compared probabilities are not equal (0.333 ≠ 0.30, or 0.15 ≠ 0.135).
criteria.evidence: Response states that the events are not independent and links this conclusion to the computed probabilities being unequal.
criteria.fix: After computing both sides of the independence check, state explicitly that unequal values mean the events are not independent.

parts.prompt: At a new location, the manager models ordering a pastry and paying with the app as independent events, with probability 0.35 that a customer orders a pastry and probability 0.50 that a customer pays with the app. Under this model, find the probability that a randomly selected customer orders a pastry and pays with the app, and the probability that the customer orders a pastry or pays with the app (or both).

criteria.text: P(pastry and app) = 0.35 × 0.50 = 0.175.
criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the two probabilities, using the stated independence, to get 0.175.
criteria.fix: For independent events, multiply the two individual probabilities to find the probability that both events occur.

criteria.evidence: Response obtains 0.675 by subtracting the joint probability from the sum of the two probabilities (or equivalently 1 − (0.65)(0.50) = 0.675).
criteria.fix: Add the two probabilities, then subtract the probability that both occur, which for independent events is their product.

item.model_answer:
(a) P(A) = 240/800 = 0.30, P(M) = 360/800 = 0.45, and P(A ∩ M) = 120/800 = 0.15.
P(A ∪ M) = P(A) + P(M) − P(A ∩ M) = 0.30 + 0.45 − 0.15 = 0.60.

(b) P(A | M) = 120/360 ≈ 0.333, while P(A) = 0.30. (Equivalently, P(A ∩ M) = 0.15 but P(A)·P(M) = 0.30 × 0.45 = 0.135.) Because P(A | M) ≠ P(A), knowing that a customer paid with the app changes the probability that the customer ordered a pastry, so A and M are not independent.

(c) Because the events are modeled as independent, P(pastry and app) = 0.35 × 0.50 = 0.175.
P(pastry or app) = 0.35 + 0.50 − 0.175 = 0.675.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction as F
T=800
PP=F(240,T);PM=F(360,T);PPM=F(120,T)
assert 120+120==240 and 240+320==560 and 120+240==360 and 120+320==440 and 240+560==800
assert PP==F(3,10) and PM==F(9,20) and PPM==F(3,20)
U=PP+PM-PPM
assert U==F(3,5) and F(120+120+240,T)==U and 1-F(320,T)==U
cond=F(120,360)
assert cond==F(1,3) and abs(float(cond)-0.333)<0.001
assert cond!=PP and PPM!=PP*PM and PP*PM==F(135,1000)
a=F(35,100);b=F(50,100)
both=a*b
assert both==F(175,1000)
assert a+b-both==F(675,1000)
assert 1-(1-a)*(1-b)==F(675,1000)
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Confidence Interval for Beetle Damage in Two Forest Sections
item.stimulus: A forestry agency wants to estimate the difference between the proportions of trees with beetle damage in the northern and southern sections of a large state forest. Each section contains more than 50,000 trees. The agency selected a random sample of 200 trees from the northern section and, independently, a random sample of 250 trees from the southern section. Of the 200 northern trees, 46 had beetle damage; of the 250 southern trees, 35 had beetle damage.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate confidence interval procedure, and define the parameter of interest in context.

criteria.text: Names a two-sample z-interval for a difference between two population proportions.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies a two-sample z-interval for p₁ − p₂ (a difference of population proportions); a one-sample interval or an interval for means does not earn the point.
criteria.fix: With two independent samples and a yes-or-no response, name the procedure as a two-sample z-interval for a difference in population proportions.

criteria.text: Defines the parameter as p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all trees in the northern section with beetle damage and p₂ is the proportion of all trees in the southern section with beetle damage.
criteria.evidence: Response defines a difference of population proportions and identifies both populations (all northern-section trees, all southern-section trees) and the response (beetle damage). Either order of subtraction earns the point if stated.
criteria.fix: Define each proportion with the response and its whole population, then state that the parameter is their difference in a stated order.

parts.prompt: The two samples were selected randomly and independently. Verify the 10% condition and the normality condition for this procedure.

criteria.text: States that each sample is at most 10% of its section: 200 and 250 are both less than 0.10(50,000) = 5,000.
criteria.evidence: Response compares each sample size with 10% of the number of trees in its section (or says each section has more than 10 times its sample size) and states that the condition is met.
criteria.fix: Compare each sample size with 10% of its own population size, using the stated number of trees in each section.

criteria.text: States that the numbers of observed successes and failures, 46, 154, 35 and 215, are all at least 10.
criteria.evidence: Response lists all four observed counts (damaged and undamaged in each sample), or n₁p̂₁, n₁(1 − p̂₁), n₂p̂₂, n₂(1 − p̂₂), and states that each is at least 10.
criteria.fix: For an interval, check all four observed counts, successes and failures in each sample, against 10.

parts.prompt: Calculate the standard error of the difference in sample proportions and a 95% confidence interval for the parameter you defined. Show your work.

criteria.evidence: Response computes each sample proportion (0.23 and 0.14) and uses each sample's own proportion in the standard error to get about 0.037; the value is the same for either order of subtraction.
criteria.fix: Compute each sample proportion first, then use each sample's own p̂ in √(p̂₁(1 − p̂₁)/n₁ + p̂₂(1 − p̂₂)/n₂).

criteria.text: 95% confidence interval: 0.09 ± 1.96(0.0370) ≈ 0.09 ± 0.0725, giving about (0.018, 0.162) for northern minus southern.
criteria.evidence: Response shows point estimate ± z* × SE with point estimate 0.23 − 0.14 = 0.09 and z* ≈ 1.96, giving about (0.018, 0.162); a stated southern-minus-northern parameter with −0.09 and about (−0.162, −0.018) also earns the point.
criteria.fix: Build the interval as point estimate ± z* × standard error, using z* = 1.96 for 95% confidence and your parameter's order.

item.model_answer:
(a) The appropriate procedure is a two-sample z-interval for a difference between two population proportions. The parameter is p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all trees in the northern section with beetle damage and p₂ is the proportion of all trees in the southern section with beetle damage.

(b) 10% condition: 200 ≤ 0.10(50,000) = 5,000 and 250 ≤ 5,000, and each section has more than 50,000 trees, so each sample is less than 10% of its section.
Normality: observed successes and failures are 46 and 200 − 46 = 154 in the northern sample and 35 and 250 − 35 = 215 in the southern sample. All four are at least 10.

(c) p̂₁ = 46/200 = 0.23 and p̂₂ = 35/250 = 0.14, so the point estimate is 0.23 − 0.14 = 0.09.
SE = √(0.23(0.77)/200 + 0.14(0.86)/250) = √(0.000886 + 0.000482) = √0.001367 ≈ 0.0370.
95% interval: 0.09 ± 1.96(0.0370) = 0.09 ± 0.0725, which is about (0.018, 0.162).
item.verification_python:
from math import sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist
x1,n1,x2,n2=46,200,35,250
p1=x1/n1;p2=x2/n2
assert abs(p1-0.23)<1e-12 and abs(p2-0.14)<1e-12
d=p1-p2
assert abs(d-0.09)<1e-12
assert n1<=0.10*50000 and n2<=0.10*50000 and abs(0.10*50000-5000)<1e-9
for c,e in zip([x1,n1-x1,x2,n2-x2],[46,154,35,215]): assert c==e and c>=10
v1=p1*(1-p1)/n1;v2=p2*(1-p2)/n2
assert abs(v1-0.000886)<5e-7 and abs(v2-0.000482)<5e-7 and abs(v1+v2-0.001367)<5e-7
se=sqrt(v1+v2)
assert abs(se-0.0370)<0.00005
z=NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975)
assert abs(z-1.96)<0.001
me=1.96*se
assert abs(me-0.0725)<0.00005
lo,hi=d-me,d+me
assert abs(lo-0.0175)<0.0001 and abs(hi-0.1625)<0.0001
assert abs(round(lo,3)-0.018)<0.0006 and abs(round(hi,3)-0.162)<1e-9
d2=p2-p1
assert abs(d2+0.09)<1e-12 and abs(sqrt(p2*(1-p2)/n2+p1*(1-p1)/n1)-se)<1e-15
assert abs((d2-me)+0.1625)<0.0001 and abs((d2+me)+0.0175)<0.0001
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Interpreting an Interval for Library Use in Two Towns
item.stimulus: A regional library board selected a random sample of 500 adult residents of Riverton and, independently, a random sample of 400 adult residents of Lakeside. Each town has more than 20,000 adult residents. In the samples, 230 of the Riverton residents (0.46) and 140 of the Lakeside residents (0.35) said they had used a public library in the past month. All conditions for inference were met, and the board calculated a 95% confidence interval for p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all adult residents of Riverton who used a public library in the past month and p₂ is the proportion of all adult residents of Lakeside who used a public library in the past month. The interval is (0.046, 0.174).

parts.prompt: Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

criteria.text: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.046 to 0.174 captures the difference (Riverton minus Lakeside) between the proportions of all adult residents of each town who used a public library in the past month.
criteria.evidence: Response says "95% confident", gives the interval limits, and describes the parameter as the difference in population proportions with the order (Riverton minus Lakeside), both towns' adult residents and library use.
criteria.fix: Name the parameter fully: the difference in the proportions of all adults in each town who used a library, and say which town is subtracted.

parts.prompt: Interpret the 95% confidence level in context.

criteria.text: Explains that if many pairs of independent random samples of 500 Riverton adults and 400 Lakeside adults were taken and a 95% interval calculated from each pair, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true difference p₁ − p₂ in the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month.
criteria.evidence: Response refers to repeated random sampling with the same sample sizes from the same two towns and states that about 95% of the resulting intervals capture the true difference, in context.
criteria.fix: Describe the long-run capture rate: in repeated random samples of the same sizes, about 95% of intervals would contain the true difference.

parts.prompt: One board member claims that the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month are different in the two towns. A second board member claims that Riverton's proportion is more than 20 percentage points higher than Lakeside's. Does the interval support each claim? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the interval supports the first claim (gives convincing evidence of a difference) because 0 is not in the interval; every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is positive.
criteria.evidence: Response notes that the interval (0.046, 0.174) does not contain 0 and concludes there is convincing evidence that the two population proportions differ.
criteria.fix: To judge a claimed difference, check whether 0 is in the interval; if 0 is excluded, there is convincing evidence of a difference.

criteria.text: States that the interval does not support the second claim because every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is less than 0.20 (0.20 is above the upper limit 0.174).
criteria.evidence: Response compares 0.20 with the interval, notes that 0.20 is not in it and that all plausible differences are below 0.20, and states that the claim is not supported.
criteria.fix: Convert percentage points to a difference, here 0.20, and check whether any plausible value in the interval is as large as that.

parts.prompt: A resident says, "Since the interval was calculated from the data, the true difference p₁ − p₂ must be between 0.046 and 0.174." Explain why the resident's statement is not correct.

criteria.text: Explains that the interval is calculated from random samples, so it may or may not contain the true difference; the 95% confidence level means about 5% of such intervals miss the true difference.
criteria.evidence: Response states that an interval based on samples might not capture p₁ − p₂, so the true difference is not guaranteed to lie between 0.046 and 0.174.
criteria.fix: Remember that confidence is not certainty: a sample-based interval may or may not contain the parameter, so never say it must be inside.

item.model_answer:
(a) We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.046 to 0.174 captures the true difference (Riverton minus Lakeside) between the proportion of all adult residents of Riverton and the proportion of all adult residents of Lakeside who used a public library in the past month.

(b) If the board took many pairs of independent random samples of 500 Riverton adults and 400 Lakeside adults and calculated a 95% confidence interval from each pair, about 95% of those intervals would capture the true difference p₁ − p₂ between the proportions of adults in the two towns who used a public library in the past month.

(c) First claim: supported. The interval (0.046, 0.174) does not contain 0, and every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is positive, so there is convincing evidence that the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month differ between the two towns.
Second claim: not supported. A difference of more than 20 percentage points means p₁ − p₂ > 0.20, but every value in the interval is less than 0.20 (the upper limit is 0.174), so a difference that large is not plausible.

(d) The interval was calculated from random samples, and a different pair of samples would give a different interval. An interval built this way may or may not contain the true difference p₁ − p₂; about 5% of 95% intervals miss it. So we can be 95% confident, but not certain, that the true difference is between 0.046 and 0.174.
item.verification_python:
from math import sqrt
x1,n1,x2,n2=230,500,140,400
p1=x1/n1;p2=x2/n2
assert abs(p1-0.46)<1e-12 and abs(p2-0.35)<1e-12
d=p1-p2
se=sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n1+p2*(1-p2)/n2)
lo,hi=d-1.96*se,d+1.96*se
assert abs(lo-0.046)<0.0005 and abs(hi-0.174)<0.0005
assert n1<=0.10*20000 and n2<=0.10*20000
for c in [x1,n1-x1,x2,n2-x2]: assert c>=10
assert not (0.046<=0<=0.174)
assert 0.174<0.20
assert abs((1-0.95)-0.05)<1e-12
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Setting Up a Test for a Bedtime Breathing Exercise
item.stimulus: A researcher recruited 180 adult volunteers who reported trouble falling asleep. The volunteers were randomly assigned to two groups of 90. Each night for two weeks, one group did a 10-minute breathing exercise at bedtime and the other group read a printed book for 10 minutes at bedtime. At the end of the two weeks, 52 of the 90 volunteers in the breathing group and 38 of the 90 volunteers in the reading group reported that they fell asleep faster. The researcher wants to know whether the data provide convincing evidence that the breathing exercise is more effective than reading at helping people like these volunteers fall asleep faster.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate testing procedure, and define the parameters of interest in context.

criteria.text: Names a two-sample z-test for a difference between two population proportions.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies a two-sample z-test for p₁ − p₂ (a difference in proportions); a one-sample test, a test for means, or a chi-square test does not earn the point.
criteria.fix: With two groups and a yes-or-no response, name the procedure as a two-sample z-test for a difference between two population proportions.

item.title: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Main News Sources
item.stimulus:
A media researcher wants to know whether the distribution of adults' main news source differs among three large cities. The researcher selected independent random samples of 150 adults from each city (each city has more than 500,000 adults) and recorded each adult's main news source. The observed counts are shown in the table, with the expected counts (calculated assuming the distribution of main news source is the same in the three cities) in parentheses.

City | Television | Online | Other | Total
City A | 60 (53.0) | 70 (77.7) | 20 (19.3) | 150
City B | 45 (53.0) | 85 (77.7) | 20 (19.3) | 150
City C | 54 (53.0) | 78 (77.7) | 18 (19.3) | 150
Total | 159 | 233 | 58 | 450

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate chi-square test, and explain why it is appropriate for this study.

criteria.text: Identifies a chi-square test for homogeneity, because the researcher took separate (independent) random samples from three populations (the adults of the three cities) and compares the distribution of one categorical variable, main news source, across those populations.
criteria.evidence: Response names the chi-square test for homogeneity and justifies it with the three separate samples from three populations and one categorical variable being compared.
criteria.fix: Use homogeneity when separate samples come from several populations and one categorical variable is compared; use independence for one sample and two variables.

parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses in context.

criteria.text: H₀: The distribution of main news source (television, online, other) is the same for adults in all three cities. Hₐ: The distribution of main news source is not the same for adults in all three cities (it differs for at least one city).
criteria.evidence: Response states a null hypothesis of no difference in the distributions of main news source across the three cities' adult populations and an alternative of a difference, both in context.
criteria.fix: Write homogeneity hypotheses about distributions of the categorical variable across populations, naming the variable and the populations, not about sample counts.

parts.prompt: The samples were independent random samples. Verify the 10% condition and the expected counts condition for the test.

criteria.text: States that each sample of 150 is at most 10% of its city's adults: 150 ≤ 0.10(500,000) = 50,000.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the sample size 150 with 10% of each city's adult population (more than 500,000) and states that the condition is met.
criteria.fix: Compare each sample size with 10% of the population it was drawn from, using the stated city population.

criteria.text: States that all expected counts are greater than 5 (the smallest is 19.3).
criteria.evidence: Response refers to the expected counts (not the observed counts) and states that all of them, including the smallest, 19.3, are greater than 5.
criteria.fix: Check the expected counts, not the observed counts, and confirm every expected count is greater than 5 by naming the smallest one.

parts.prompt: If the null hypothesis is true, the test statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Describe the shape of this distribution and how it compares with the shape of a chi-square distribution with 10 degrees of freedom. Then explain what a large value of the chi-square statistic would indicate about the observed counts compared with the expected counts.

criteria.text: States that the chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom is skewed right, and that the distribution with 10 degrees of freedom is less skewed (its skew is less pronounced).
criteria.evidence: Response describes the 4-degree-of-freedom distribution as skewed right and says the 10-degree-of-freedom distribution is less strongly skewed; stating that the values are positive is not required.
criteria.fix: Recall that chi-square distributions are skewed right and become less skewed as the degrees of freedom increase.

criteria.text: Explains that the chi-square statistic measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to the expected counts, so a large value indicates that the observed counts are far from the counts expected if the distributions were the same.
criteria.evidence: Response states that a large chi-square value means the observed counts differ greatly from the expected counts (relative to the expected counts).
criteria.fix: Link the statistic to its formula: each term compares an observed count with its expected count, so large values mean large departures.

item.model_answer:
(a) The appropriate test is a chi-square test for homogeneity. The researcher took three separate, independent random samples from three populations (the adults of City A, City B and City C) and wants to compare the distribution of one categorical variable, main news source, across those populations.

(b) H₀: The distribution of main news source (television, online, other) is the same for adults in City A, City B and City C.
Hₐ: The distribution of main news source is not the same for adults in all three cities.

(c) 10% condition: each sample of 150 adults is less than 10% of its city's adults, because 0.10(500,000) = 50,000 and 150 ≤ 50,000.
Expected counts: all nine expected counts (53.0, 77.7 and 19.3 for each city) are greater than 5; the smallest is 19.3.

(d) The approximate null distribution, chi-square with 4 degrees of freedom, takes only positive values and is skewed right. A chi-square distribution with 10 degrees of freedom is also skewed right, but its skew is less pronounced.
The chi-square statistic adds up (observed − expected)²/expected over all the cells, so it measures how far the observed counts are from the expected counts relative to the expected counts. A large value would indicate that the observed counts are far from the counts expected if the distribution of main news source were the same in all three cities.

item.title: Comparing Two Estimators of a Germination Proportion
item.stimulus:
A seed company wants to estimate p, the proportion of all seeds in a large bin that germinate. Two estimators are proposed, each based on a random sample of 10 seeds, where X is the number of sampled seeds that germinate.

Estimator A: X/10 (the sample proportion)
Estimator B: (X + 2)/14

To study the estimators, a statistics class used a computer to simulate 1,000 random samples of 10 seeds from a large bin in which exactly 40% of the seeds germinate. For each simulated sample, the class calculated the value of both estimators. The results are summarized in the table.

Estimator | Mean of the 1,000 simulated values
A | 0.401
B | 0.429

parts.prompt: Based on the simulation, which estimator appears to be unbiased and which appears to be biased? Justify your answers.

criteria.text: Identifies Estimator A as appearing unbiased because the mean of its simulated values, 0.401, is approximately equal to the true proportion, 0.40.
criteria.evidence: Response compares the mean of A's simulated values (0.401) with p = 0.40, states that they are approximately equal, and so A does not tend to overestimate or underestimate p.
criteria.fix: Judge bias by comparing the center (mean) of the estimator's simulated values with the true parameter used in the simulation, here 0.40.

criteria.text: Identifies Estimator B as biased because the mean of its simulated values, 0.429, is greater than 0.40, so on average B overestimates the true proportion.
criteria.evidence: Response states that B is biased and explains that its simulated values are centered above 0.40, so it tends to overestimate p.
criteria.fix: When simulated values center above or below the true parameter, call the estimator biased and name the direction: overestimates or underestimates.

parts.prompt: The company then selects a random sample of 10 seeds from a new bin whose germination proportion is unknown, and 7 of the 10 seeds germinate. Calculate the value of each estimator for this sample, and identify which value the company should report as an unbiased point estimate of the proportion of all seeds in the new bin that germinate.

criteria.text: Calculates Estimator A = 7/10 = 0.70.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes X = 7 into X/10 to get 0.70.
criteria.fix: Substitute the observed count X into each estimator's formula exactly as written, then simplify.

criteria.text: Calculates Estimator B = (7 + 2)/14 = 9/14 ≈ 0.643.
criteria.evidence: Response substitutes X = 7 into (X + 2)/14 to get 9/14, about 0.643.
criteria.fix: Add 2 to the observed count before dividing by 14; do not divide by the sample size 10.

criteria.text: Identifies 0.70, the value of Estimator A (the sample proportion), as the unbiased point estimate to report.
criteria.evidence: Response names the value of Estimator A as the unbiased point estimate, because A was the estimator shown to be unbiased.
criteria.fix: Report the value from the estimator the simulation showed to be unbiased, here the sample proportion X/10.

parts.prompt: A student says, "Because Estimator A is unbiased, its value from any single sample will be closer to the true proportion than the value of Estimator B." Explain why the student's statement is incorrect.

criteria.text: Explains that unbiased describes the average of the estimator's values over many random samples, so in a particular sample the value of Estimator A can be farther from the true proportion than the value of Estimator B.
criteria.evidence: Response states that unbiasedness refers to the estimator's values on average across repeated samples, not to the accuracy of one sample's value, so A can miss p by more than B in a given sample.
criteria.fix: Remember unbiased means correct on average across many samples; state that the value from one sample can still miss the parameter by more.

item.model_answer:
(a) Estimator A appears to be unbiased. In the simulation the true proportion was 0.40, and the mean of A's 1,000 simulated values is 0.401, which is approximately 0.40, so on average A neither overestimates nor underestimates p.
Estimator B appears to be biased. The mean of its simulated values is 0.429, which is clearly greater than 0.40, so on average B overestimates the true proportion of seeds that germinate.

(b) Estimator A: 7/10 = 0.70. Estimator B: (7 + 2)/14 = 9/14 ≈ 0.643.
The company should report 0.70, the value of Estimator A (the sample proportion), as the unbiased point estimate of the proportion of all seeds in the new bin that germinate.

(c) Unbiased means that the values of Estimator A are centered at the true proportion on average over many random samples. It does not mean that the value from a single sample is close to p, or closer than B's value. For example, if p = 0.40 and a sample has X = 7, Estimator A gives 0.70 (0.30 away from 0.40) while Estimator B gives about 0.643 (about 0.243 away), so in that sample A is farther from the true proportion.

item.title: Interpreting a Poll Interval for a Ballot Measure
item.stimulus: A polling organization selected a random sample of 400 registered voters from a state with about 6 million registered voters. Of the voters sampled, 224 said they support a proposed ballot measure. All conditions for inference were met, and the organization reported a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all the state's registered voters who support the measure: (0.511, 0.609).

parts.prompt: Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

criteria.text: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.511 to 0.609 captures the proportion of all registered voters in the state who support the ballot measure.
criteria.evidence: Response says "95% confident" that the interval (0.511, 0.609) contains the true (population) proportion and identifies the population (all the state's registered voters) and the response (support for the measure).
criteria.fix: Name the parameter fully: the proportion of all registered voters in this state who support the measure, not the 400 sampled voters.

parts.prompt: Interpret the 95% confidence level in context.

criteria.text: Explains that if many random samples of 400 registered voters were taken from this state and a 95% confidence interval were calculated from each, about 95% of those intervals would capture the proportion of all the state's registered voters who support the measure.
criteria.evidence: Response refers to repeated random samples of the same size and states that about 95% of the resulting intervals capture the population proportion, in context.
criteria.fix: Describe the long-run capture rate: in many repeated random samples of 400 voters, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true proportion.

parts.prompt: Supporters of the measure claim that a majority of the state's registered voters support it. The measure's sponsor claims that 65% of the state's registered voters support it. Does the interval support each claim? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the interval supports the majority claim (provides convincing evidence for it) because every value in the interval from 0.511 to 0.609 is greater than 0.50.
criteria.evidence: Response notes that all plausible values in the interval are above 0.50, so the claim that a majority support the measure is supported.
criteria.fix: Check where 0.50 lies relative to the whole interval; if every plausible value is above it, the majority claim is supported.

criteria.text: States that the interval does not support the 65% claim because 0.65 is not in the interval; every plausible value is less than 0.65.
criteria.evidence: Response observes that 0.65 is greater than the upper limit 0.609, so 0.65 is not a plausible value of the population proportion.
criteria.fix: Check whether the claimed value lies inside the interval; a value outside the interval is not a plausible value of the parameter.

parts.prompt: Answer each question about how the interval would change. First, if the organization had used a 99% confidence level with the same sample, would the margin of error be larger, smaller, or the same? Explain. Second, if the organization had instead used a random sample of 1,600 registered voters and obtained the same sample proportion, about how would the width of the 95% confidence interval compare with the width of (0.511, 0.609)?

criteria.text: States that the margin of error would be larger because a 99% confidence level uses a larger critical value (z* ≈ 2.576 instead of 1.96).
criteria.evidence: Response answers larger and attributes the change to the larger critical value required for a higher confidence level.
criteria.fix: Recall that raising the confidence level raises the critical value z*, which increases the margin of error for the same sample.

criteria.text: States that the width would be about half as large (about 0.049 instead of 0.098), because the width is approximately proportional to 1/√n and √(1,600/400) = 2.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the interval would be about half as wide and links this to the sample size being 4 times as large (width proportional to 1/√n).
criteria.fix: Use width ∝ 1/√n: multiplying the sample size by 4 divides the width by √4 = 2.

item.model_answer:
(a) We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.511 to 0.609 captures the true proportion of all registered voters in the state who support the proposed ballot measure.

(b) If the organization took many random samples of 400 registered voters from this state and calculated a 95% confidence interval from each sample, about 95% of those intervals would capture the true proportion of all the state's registered voters who support the measure.

(c) Majority claim: supported. Every value in the interval, from 0.511 to 0.609, is greater than 0.50, so the interval gives convincing evidence that a majority of the state's registered voters support the measure.
65% claim: not supported. The value 0.65 is greater than the upper limit 0.609, so 0.65 is not a plausible value for the proportion of all registered voters who support the measure; all plausible values are less than 0.65.

(d) The margin of error would be larger. A 99% confidence level requires a larger critical value (z* ≈ 2.576 instead of z* ≈ 1.96), and the margin of error is the critical value times the standard error, which stays the same for the same sample.
With 1,600 voters the interval would be about half as wide. The width is approximately proportional to 1/√n, and √(1,600/400) = √4 = 2, so the width would be about 0.098/2 ≈ 0.049 instead of 0.609 − 0.511 = 0.098.

item.title: Setting Up a Test for Streetlight Outages
item.stimulus: A city reports that 10% of its 9,400 streetlights are out of service. After a new repair program, the city's public works department believes that the proportion of the city's streetlights that are out of service has decreased. An inspector checks a random sample of 120 of the city's streetlights and finds that 9 of them are out of service. The department plans to use these data to test its belief.

parts.prompt: Identify the appropriate testing procedure, and define the parameter of interest in context.

criteria.text: Names a one-sample z-test for a population proportion.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies a one-sample z-test for a (single) population proportion; naming a test for a mean or a two-sample procedure does not earn the point.
criteria.fix: With one sample and a yes-or-no response, name the procedure as a one-sample z-test for a population proportion.

criteria.text: Defines p as the proportion of all the city's streetlights that are out of service (after the repair program).
criteria.evidence: Response defines the parameter as a proportion that refers to all of the city's streetlights and to being out of service, not to the 120 sampled lights or the count of 9.
criteria.fix: Define p with three pieces: a proportion, the response (out of service), and the population (all of the city's streetlights).

parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for the department's test.

criteria.text: H₀: p = 0.10 (or H₀: p ≥ 0.10, tested at 0.10) and Hₐ: p < 0.10.
criteria.evidence: Response writes the null hypothesis at the value 0.10 (p = 0.10, or p ≥ 0.10 as the CED permits for a one-sided test) and a one-sided alternative p < 0.10, both in terms of the population proportion p (not p̂).
criteria.fix: Put the status quo value in H₀ with an equals sign and the department's belief (a decrease) in Hₐ using <.

parts.prompt: Verify the randomization condition and the 10% condition for this test.

criteria.text: States that the randomization condition is met because the inspector checked a random sample of the city's streetlights.
criteria.evidence: Response cites the random sample of 120 streetlights as meeting the randomization condition.
criteria.fix: For the randomization condition, quote the random selection described in the study and say what was randomly selected.

criteria.text: States that the 10% condition is met because 120 ≤ 0.10(9,400) = 940 (equivalently, 9,400 ≥ 10 × 120 = 1,200).
criteria.evidence: Response compares the sample size 120 with 10% of the 9,400 streetlights (or compares 9,400 with 10 × 120) and states the condition is met.
criteria.fix: Show the 10% condition with numbers: compare the sample size with 10% of the stated population size.

parts.prompt: A classmate says that the normality condition for this test is not met because only 9 of the sampled streetlights were out of service. Is the classmate correct? Explain.

criteria.text: States that the classmate is not correct because the test's normality condition uses the null value p₀ = 0.10: np₀ = 120(0.10) = 12 and n(1 − p₀) = 120(0.90) = 108 are both at least 10.
criteria.evidence: Response says the classmate is incorrect and checks the expected counts 12 and 108 using p₀ = 0.10, both at least 10.
criteria.fix: For a test, check the normality condition with expected counts np₀ and n(1 − p₀), not with the observed counts.

item.model_answer:
(a) The appropriate procedure is a one-sample z-test for a population proportion. Let p = the proportion of all the city's streetlights that are out of service (after the repair program).

(b) H₀: p = 0.10
Hₐ: p < 0.10

(c) Randomization: the inspector checked a random sample of 120 of the city's streetlights, so the randomization condition is met.
10% condition: the sample of 120 streetlights is less than 10% of the city's 9,400 streetlights, because 0.10 × 9,400 = 940 and 120 ≤ 940, so the condition is met.

(d) The classmate is not correct. In a significance test the normality condition is checked using the null value p₀ = 0.10, because the test assumes H₀ is true. The expected number of out-of-service lights is np₀ = 120(0.10) = 12 and the expected number in service is n(1 − p₀) = 120(0.90) = 108. Both are at least 10, so the normality condition is met.

item.title: Sampling Distribution of a Difference in On-Campus Housing Rates
item.stimulus: At University X, which has 18,000 students, 62% of the students live on campus. At University Y, which has 25,000 students, 48% of the students live on campus. A researcher will select a random sample of 120 students from University X and, independently, a random sample of 100 students from University Y. Let p̂₁ be the proportion of the sampled University X students who live on campus, and let p̂₂ be the proportion of the sampled University Y students who live on campus.

parts.prompt: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂.

criteria.evidence: Response gives the mean as the difference in population proportions, 0.62 − 0.48 = 0.14.
criteria.fix: The sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂ is centered at p₁ − p₂; subtract the two population proportions in the same order.

criteria.evidence: Response adds the two variance terms p(1 − p)/n under one square root, using 0.62 with 120 and 0.48 with 100, to get about 0.0668.
criteria.fix: Add the variances p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ and p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂, then take the square root; never subtract them or add standard deviations.

parts.prompt: The two samples will be independent random samples. Verify the remaining conditions that justify using this standard deviation formula and modeling the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂ as approximately normal.

criteria.text: States that each sample is at most 10% of its population: 120 ≤ 0.10(18,000) = 1,800 and 100 ≤ 0.10(25,000) = 2,500.
criteria.evidence: Response compares each sample size with 10% of its own university's enrollment and states that the 10% condition is met for both samples.
criteria.fix: Check the 10% condition separately for each sample, comparing each sample size with 10% of its own population size.

criteria.text: States that n₁p₁ = 74.4, n₁(1 − p₁) = 45.6, n₂p₂ = 48 and n₂(1 − p₂) = 52 are all at least 10, so the sampling distribution is approximately normal.
criteria.evidence: Response computes all four expected counts using the population proportions (74.4, 45.6, 48, 52) and states that each is at least 10.
criteria.fix: List all four expected counts, successes and failures for each sample, and confirm that each one is at least 10.

parts.prompt: Find the probability that the proportion of sampled University X students who live on campus is less than the proportion of sampled University Y students who live on campus. Show your work.

criteria.text: Identifies the event as p̂₁ − p̂₂ < 0 and uses a normal model with mean 0.14 and standard deviation 0.0668, for example z = (0 − 0.14)/0.0668 ≈ −2.10.
criteria.evidence: Response shows the event p̂₁ − p̂₂ < 0 with the normal model's mean 0.14 and standard deviation about 0.0668, either as a z-score or as labeled technology inputs.
criteria.fix: Translate the comparison into p̂₁ − p̂₂ < 0, then standardize the boundary 0 using the mean and standard deviation found earlier.

criteria.text: Finds the probability ≈ 0.018.
criteria.evidence: Response reports a probability of about 0.018 (0.0179 to 0.0180).
criteria.fix: After finding z ≈ −2.10, use the standard normal table or technology for the area to the left, not the right.

item.model_answer:
(a) Mean: μ(p̂₁ − p̂₂) = p₁ − p₂ = 0.62 − 0.48 = 0.14.
Standard deviation: σ(p̂₁ − p̂₂) = √(0.62(0.38)/120 + 0.48(0.52)/100) = √(0.001963 + 0.002496) = √0.004459 ≈ 0.0668.

(b) The 10% condition holds for each sample: 120 ≤ 0.10(18,000) = 1,800 and 100 ≤ 0.10(25,000) = 2,500, so the standard deviation formula applies.
Large counts: n₁p₁ = 120(0.62) = 74.4, n₁(1 − p₁) = 120(0.38) = 45.6, n₂p₂ = 100(0.48) = 48 and n₂(1 − p₂) = 100(0.52) = 52. All four are at least 10, so the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂ is approximately normal.

(c) The event is p̂₁ < p̂₂, that is, p̂₁ − p̂₂ < 0. Using the normal model with mean 0.14 and standard deviation 0.0668:
z = (0 − 0.14)/0.0668 ≈ −2.10, and P(Z < −2.10) ≈ 0.018.
There is about a 0.018 probability that the sample proportion of University X students who live on campus is less than the sample proportion of University Y students who live on campus.
item.verification_python:
from math import sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist
p1,p2,n1,n2=0.62,0.48,120,100
m=p1-p2
assert abs(m-0.14)<1e-12
v1=p1*(1-p1)/n1;v2=p2*(1-p2)/n2
assert abs(v1-0.001963)<5e-7 and abs(v2-0.002496)<5e-7 and abs(v1+v2-0.004459)<5e-7
sd=sqrt(v1+v2)
assert abs(sd-0.0668)<0.00005
assert n1<=0.10*18000 and abs(0.10*18000-1800)<1e-9
assert n2<=0.10*25000 and abs(0.10*25000-2500)<1e-9
c=[n1*p1,n1*(1-p1),n2*p2,n2*(1-p2)]
for a,b in zip(c,[74.4,45.6,48,52]): assert abs(a-b)<1e-9 and a>=10
z=(0-m)/sd
assert abs(z-(-2.10))<0.005
P=NormalDist(m,sd).cdf(0)
assert abs(P-0.018)<0.0005
assert abs(NormalDist().cdf(-2.10)-0.0179)<0.0001
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
